headline: With the 10Y pinned near 5.14%, a December hike ≈94% priced and DXY at a 19-month high, Warsh's noon-ET framing of AI as productivity or as overheating sets the tone for a week that runs through retail sales, Nvidia, the FOMC minutes, a 20Y auction and the Anthropic IPO.
summary: Overnight tape: Nasdaq-100 futures fell ≈0.8–1.0% and S&P futures ≈0.2–0.3%, while Dow futures were flat to +0.1% (≈52,400–52,460), so the AI-heavy names are leading lower again before Nvidia reports Tuesday. The 10Y is holding ≈5.13–5.15% after a +29bp five-session run. DXY is ≈103.46, its highest since Apr 2025 after five straight up days. Gold dipped to $3,832 in Asia, its lowest since Oct 2025, before rebounding to ≈$3,870.

Fed: fed funds futures put ≈93–94% on a 25bp hike at the Dec 8–9 FOMC, and the remainder is a 50bp bet. Weekend FedWatch reads also show ≈67% for another hike in January and ≈63% for March. Warsh opens the SF Fed Productivity & Jobs Task Force conference at 11:00 AM CT. Previews expect him to avoid pre-committing, but any line casting the AI capex boom as demand pressure rather than supply would add to 2027 SOFR hike pricing. Goolsbee said last week that inflation is 'going the wrong way' and that 'everything is always on the table.'

Global growth weakened overnight. China's October data missed on all three measures: IP +4.8% y/y (5.3% expected), retail sales +0.4% (0.8%), and Jan–Oct FAI −8.1% (−7.0%), with property investment down ≈21.6%. Japan's Q3 GDP fell 0.1% annualized against +0.3% expected, its first contraction in a year, but December BOJ hike odds are still ≈76% (LSEG). Weak demand abroad with hot US inflation is a strong-dollar, weak-metals mix.

Metals and energy: LME copper fell to ≈$13,251/t from $13,588 (SP Angel) on the China miss and the tech selloff. Silver is ≈$47.3, down from $49.15 Friday, and platinum is ≈$1,473. Oil barely moved after Iran struck a US helicopter base in Bahrain on Sunday and claimed five vessels hit mines near Hormuz: Brent is ≈$95.5–96.3 and WTI ≈$88.5. The market is pricing the Gulf risk as contained.

Equity and AI news: per WSJ-sourced reports, the White House plans to name 20+ AI 'national champions' (Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic) to fast-track their overseas expansion, with Lutnick possibly announcing within a week. Nvidia (interim CEO Kress) still faces Bessent's 10-day demand for answers and HSBC's downgrade to Hold with a $170 target. Options price an ≈8–11% move for Tuesday's print. Anthropic is set to price on Wed (range $70–78, 825M shares) and trade Thursday as ANT.

Today's calendar: Empire State at 7:30 AM CT (consensus 17.6, prior 25.5; watch prices paid, prior 59.5), NAHB at 9:00, Warsh at 11:00, and the 13F deadline after the close. Tomorrow brings Oct retail sales, IP and Nvidia. On Wednesday the $16B 20Y auction (the Aug 20Y cleared 5.204%) comes ahead of the Oct FOMC minutes.
markets_asof: ≈3:00 PM CT close (equities, Treasuries); gold 12:47 PM CT; silver, copper, oil are midday reads

calendar.why: The first November factory print. Prices paid (prior 59.5) and prices received (30.6) matter more than the headline for a Fed already hiking.
Shows how builders are coping with the 10Y above 5% and mortgage rates rising with it.

calendar.event: Fed Chair Warsh opens the Productivity & Jobs Task Force conference (SF Fed, livestreamed)
calendar.prior: Jackson Hole: hinted hikes may be needed
calendar.why: His first remarks since hot CPI/PPI. Framing AI as a productivity gain would ease 2027 hike pricing, while framing it as overheating demand would cheapen the SOFR strip. He is also expected to discuss shrinking forward guidance.

calendar.event: Warsh fireside chat with Marc Andreessen and Gina Raimondo (conference close)
calendar.why: An unscripted Q&A carries a higher risk of headlines than the prepared remarks.

calendar.event: 13F filing deadline (Q3 holdings, incl. Berkshire Hathaway)
calendar.why: Shows whether big holders cut AI and bank exposure in Q3, which is useful context for both bank stocks and NVDA.
The week's main data test. A strong control group would support a 50bp argument in December.

calendar.event: Nvidia FQ3 earnings (first since Huang's resignation)
calendar.why: A ≈$300B+ market-cap swing either way that sets the tone for Anthropic's pricing.
Another tail would push the 30Y through 5.50%. The minutes show how many members besides dissenters Cook and Hammack wanted to hike in October.
The question is no longer whether the Fed hikes but how much (25 vs 50bp) and how many more it signals for 2027.

rates.title: 10Y holds above 5.1% after a +29bp week; long end leads
rates.body: The 10Y is ≈5.14% after rising 29bp in five sessions. The 30Y closed last week at ≈5.47% (+21bp), after a weak $30B 30Y auction that needed 5.44% to clear, and PPI ran at a 6.5% annual rate, the hottest since Nov 2022. FNArena calls the Nov 6–13 move a front-end-led bear flattener, while others see fiscal term premium driving the long end, so the curve-shape debate is live.
rates.simple: A Treasury yield is the interest rate the US government pays to borrow. It rises when investors demand more to hold its bonds. Yields jumped last week because inflation came in hot and buyers at the government's bond sales were scarce. Higher Treasury yields feed straight into mortgage, car-loan and corporate borrowing costs.
rates.source: Wolf Street / FNArena / Seoul Economic Daily

rates.title: December hike ≈94% priced; January and March also leaning to hikes
rates.body: Fed funds futures put ≈93.9% on +25bp on Dec 9, and the remainder is a 50bp bet. Weekend FedWatch reads showed ≈67% for another hike in January and ≈63% for March. Goolsbee (a 2027 voter) called October CPI 'concerning' and said 'everything is always on the table', and Waller has said he is open to 50bp if the data support it.
rates.simple: Traders bet on future Fed moves through futures contracts, and those prices are converted into probabilities. The market now treats a December rate increase as almost certain and expects more early next year. Each increase raises the floor under borrowing costs and the interest savers earn.
rates.source: Reuters via CNBC / Motley Fool / Quartz

rates.title: Japan contracts, China slows: growth abroad weakens as US inflation runs hot
rates.body: Japan's Q3 GDP fell 0.1% annualized against +0.3% expected, with consumption down 0.3% q/q for a second straight quarter and net exports cutting 0.6pp. LSEG still puts ≈76% on a December BOJ hike, and USD/JPY is ≈159.7 after touching 160.19 on Friday. China missed on IP, retail sales and FAI.
rates.simple: Gross domestic product (GDP) is the total value of what an economy produces. Japan's shrank slightly as costly energy imports and squeezed shoppers weighed on growth. When other major economies weaken while US inflation stays high, money flows into the dollar and US assets, which strengthens the dollar and makes imports cheaper for Americans but US exports pricier abroad.

derivatives.title: SOFR strip repriced hawkish; Dec-27 contract is doing the work
derivatives.body: After CPI, the rate implied by Dec-2027 SOFR futures jumped 21.5bp to ≈4.63%, versus +12bp to ≈4.29% for Dec-2026. That means the market is adding hikes deep into 2027 rather than just pulling December forward. Warsh at 11 AM CT and Wednesday's minutes are the catalysts for the Dec26/Dec27 spread.
derivatives.simple: SOFR futures are CME contracts that let traders bet on or hedge the overnight interest rate banks pay on secured loans. Their price shows where the market thinks rates will be on a future date. The biggest moves are in contracts for late 2027, so traders think the Fed will keep raising rates for longer, not just once.

derivatives.title: CME posts record October: 30M contracts/day, Treasury F&O +48%
derivatives.body: CME's October ADV was a record 30M contracts (+15% y/y), with records in interest-rate, equity-index, energy and ag products. Treasury futures and options ADV rose 48%. With the rates selloff extending into November, Q4 volume is on course to stay elevated, and CME declared a $1.30 quarterly dividend payable Dec 30.
derivatives.simple: Average daily volume (ADV) counts how many futures and options contracts change hands on a typical day. Volume jumps when uncertainty about rates rises, because banks, funds and companies rush to hedge, and CME earns a fee on every contract. Volatile bond markets are good business for Chicago's exchange.

derivatives.title: Nvidia options imply the largest earnings move since 2024
derivatives.body: Estimates of the implied move for Tuesday's print range from ≈7.3% (Unusual Whales) to ≈10.8% (EarningsWatcher). Benzinga had ≈9.6% as of Nov 12 and put the swing at ≈$341B of market cap. HSBC cut NVDA to Hold with a $170 target, ≈4% above Friday's close, and Bernstein halved its target to $200.
derivatives.simple: An implied move is the size of the stock jump or drop, in either direction, that option prices suggest after earnings. Traders are paying up for protection because Nvidia just lost its founder-CEO and faces political pressure. Because Nvidia is such a large weight in the indexes, its swing moves most people's retirement funds.

metals.title: Gold tests $3,832, lowest since Oct 2025, as real yields and the dollar squeeze it
metals.body: Spot gold hit $3,832 in early Asia before rebounding to ≈$3,872, after a −4.3% week to $3,885.60. With the 10Y above 5%, 10Y TIPS real yields near ≈2.9% and DXY at a 19-month high, gold faces its two biggest opposing forces at once. SCMP says gold is now down >9% YTD and on track to snap a three-year winning streak, and central-bank buying is the remaining support.
metals.simple: Gold pays no interest, so when safe bonds pay a high real yield (interest after inflation), holding gold costs more in lost income. A stronger dollar also makes gold pricier for foreign buyers. Both forces are at multi-year extremes, which is why gold is sliding even with a war in the Gulf.

metals.title: Copper and silver drop on China's triple miss
metals.body: SP Angel puts LME copper at ≈$13,251/t, down from $13,588, with silver ≈$47.3/oz and platinum ≈$1,473. China's October IP rose 4.8% (5.3% expected), Jan–Oct property investment fell ≈21.6% and new starts fell 24.4%. Physical tightness persists: China's concentrate imports fell 11% in October and the Yangshan premium hit a record $230/t.
metals.simple: China buys roughly half the world's copper, much of it for buildings, power grids and factories. Weak Chinese factory and property numbers mean less expected demand, so prices fell. Mine supply is tight at the same time, so dips could be short-lived, which matters for anyone hedging metal costs.
metals.source: SP Angel via Share-Talk / CNBC / MINING.COM

banking.title: Hancock Whitney to buy Trustmark for ≈$3.2B in stock
banking.body: The all-stock deal, announced Nov 12, creates an ≈$58B-asset Southeastern lender across six states. Closing is targeted for late Q1 2027, pending approvals. The Fed's NIC counts 162 bank mergers in 2026 through Nov 2, the largest being Santander's absorption of Webster ($85.9B in assets).
banking.simple: An all-stock deal means the buyer pays with its own shares instead of cash. Mid-size banks are merging to spread rising tech and compliance costs over a bigger customer base, and regulators are approving deals faster than in past years. For customers that can mean fewer branches but larger lending limits.

banking.title: Anthropic IPO: $70–78 range, 825M shares, books covered; trading expected Thu
banking.body: The range implies ≈$64B in primary proceeds at the top, before a 123.75M-share greenshoe and a reported $26B Class N private placement. Valuation is ≈$0.92–1.02T on outstanding shares or up to ≈$1.4T fully diluted. Goldman and Morgan Stanley lead a 22-bank syndicate, and the FT reported over the weekend that pricing above the range is under discussion.
banking.simple: In an IPO, banks gauge investor demand and set the price at which a private company first sells shares to the public. A greenshoe is an option for the banks to sell extra shares if demand is strong. This would be one of the largest share sales ever, and the fees and trading activity are a big payday for Wall Street's capital-markets desks.

banking.title: Bank stocks firm into the selloff: KBW Bank Index +0.6% Friday
banking.body: BKX closed at 175.28 (+0.60%) and the regional KRX at 141.02 (+0.26%), while the Nasdaq fell 0.9%. BKX is still ≈10% below its Aug 17 high of 195.55. A steeper long end helps net interest margins, but 5%+ yields add to unrealized securities losses and CRE refinancing stress.
banking.simple: Banks profit from the gap between what they earn on loans and what they pay on deposits, called net interest margin. Higher long-term rates can widen that gap, which is why bank stocks rose on a down day. Those same higher rates lower the value of bonds banks already own and make it harder for borrowers to refinance.

banking.title: White House to tap 20+ AI 'national champions' for export and financing support
banking.body: Per WSJ-sourced reports, Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic are among the companies expected to get faster export licenses, help with overseas operations and possible access to federal (EXIM) financing. Commerce Secretary Lutnick could announce within a week. It builds on the July 2025 American AI Exports Program.
banking.simple: A 'national champion' is a company a government chooses to back so it can win business abroad. Here that could mean faster permission to sell chips and AI services overseas and government-backed loans for foreign buyers. That would support these firms' revenue and bring new export-finance deals to banks.

cnbc.title: Futures mixed as Nvidia and the Anthropic debut loom
cnbc.body: Nasdaq-100 futures fell 0.79% and S&P futures 0.25% early Monday, after all three indexes gained more than 2% last week, their best since August. Tech is lagging on Nvidia's leadership vacuum before Tuesday's print.
cnbc.simple: Stock futures trade before the market opens and give an early read on the day. Investors are cautious on tech because Nvidia, the market's biggest AI company, has lost its CEO right before reporting earnings. Last week's rally makes stocks more vulnerable to bad news.

cnbc.title: China's slowdown deepens in October
cnbc.body: IP +4.8% y/y, retail sales +0.4% and FAI −8.1% YTD all missed, with retail weak despite Singles Day. New home prices fell for a 41st straight month (−0.15% m/m).
cnbc.simple: These are China's monthly reports on factory output, shop spending and investment, and all three came in below forecasts. Chinese households are still nervous after years of falling home prices, and they are spending less. That weighs on global demand for metals, oil and US exports.

cnbc.title: Japan's economy contracts in Q3
cnbc.body: Real GDP fell 0.1% annualized against +0.3% expected, its first drop in a year, as energy imports and weak consumption weighed. Yen ≈159.7/$.
cnbc.simple: Japan's economy shrank slightly last quarter because expensive imported oil and squeezed households cut into growth. A weak yen makes the energy problem worse. Japan's central bank may now hesitate to raise rates, which keeps the yen weak against the dollar.

cnbc.title: Markets spooked as a supersized December hike enters the conversation
cnbc.body: After hot October CPI, a 50bp December hike went from zero to ≈11–14% odds, and Waller signaled he is open to it. The current split is ≈94% for 25bp and ≈6% for 50bp.
cnbc.simple: The Fed normally moves rates in quarter-point steps, so a half-point move would signal alarm about inflation. Even a small chance of one pushes up borrowing costs across the economy. That is a big reason stocks and bonds were volatile last week.

wsj.title: Trump administration plans to name AI 'national champions'
wsj.body: More than two dozen AI firms, including Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic, would be designated to support their overseas expansion. Benefits could include faster export licenses and federal financing.
wsj.simple: The government plans to pick favored US AI companies and help them sell abroad, much as other countries back their national industries. That could speed up chip and cloud exports. It also makes those companies' fortunes more tied to Washington's policy choices.

wsj.title: Bessent urges Nvidia's board to hire an outside CEO
wsj.body: The Treasury Secretary wants an external successor to Huang and demanded answers 'in the next 10 days' tied to China chip-sale compliance. A petition to reinstate Huang passed 106,000 names, and the FT reports the board approached Arm's Rene Haas.
wsj.simple: It is unusual for a top government official to tell a private company whom to hire. The pressure stems from concerns about Nvidia chips reaching China. Uncertainty about who will run the world's most valuable chipmaker is weighing on its stock and the wider market.

wsj.title: Boeing-Lockheed rocket failure destroys Amazon satellite payload
wsj.body: A US rocket failed mid-flight, destroying a batch of Amazon's Leo internet satellites (MarketScreener puts it at 40). It is a setback for Amazon's broadband constellation build-out.
wsj.simple: Amazon is launching thousands of satellites to sell space-based internet. Losing a full batch costs money and time and delays its race against SpaceX's Starlink. It also raises insurance and launch-cost questions for the whole space industry.

tribune.title: FAA ground stop strands O'Hare: 700+ Friday cancellations, United pulls flights through Sunday
tribune.body: The longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years canceled 700+ O'Hare flights Friday and 14,000+ nationally Friday–Saturday. United, which is Chicago-based, requested a separate O'Hare inbound hold Saturday and cancelled most of its remaining Sunday-night flights. The FAA expects schedules to be normal by end of Sunday.
tribune.simple: A ground stop means the FAA holds planes on the ground because it cannot safely manage traffic, this time due to failed equipment. United's main hub is O'Hare, so it takes a big revenue and cost hit. Expect pressure on Congress to fund air-traffic-control upgrades.

tribune.title: Chicago Fed's Goolsbee: inflation 'going the wrong way'
tribune.body: Goolsbee called October CPI 'another concerning report' and blamed sticky tariff goods prices, AI data-center demand, and services and healthcare costs. He would not rule out a larger hike, and he speaks again Thursday in Indianapolis. He votes on the FOMC in 2027.
tribune.simple: Goolsbee runs the Chicago Fed and is usually one of the more cautious voices on raising rates. When even he sounds worried about inflation, markets read it as a sign the Fed will keep tightening. That means higher borrowing costs for Midwest businesses and households.

tribune.title: CME Group: record October volume, $1.30 dividend
tribune.body: ADV hit a record 30M contracts (+15% y/y), with US Treasury F&O up 48%, and lean hogs set a daily record of 209,363 contracts on Nov 11. CME closed Friday at $317.97.
tribune.simple: CME is the Chicago exchange where interest-rate, stock-index, energy and farm futures trade. When markets are turbulent, more people hedge, and CME collects more fees. Its record month shows how much the bond-market selloff has raised demand for protection.

tribune.title: Loop office distress: Wacker Drive tower sells at ≈75% discount
tribune.body: A local investor group bought a Wacker Drive office tower for $30M, ≈75% below its prior value, and a 27-story Mag Mile office high-rise is headed to auction.
tribune.simple: Many downtown office buildings are worth far less than before the pandemic because fewer people work there. Selling at a deep discount means lenders and owners take large losses. Banks with heavy commercial real estate loans are exposed when this happens.
tribune.source: The Real Deal Chicago / Connect CRE

nyt.title: Aging air-traffic system behind the nationwide ground stop
nyt.body: The Times reports the FAA's control system has had several disruptive failures in recent months. Duffy blamed 'old switches, old routers', warned 'you will have more of these' without an upgrade, and is seeking billions in aviation funding.
nyt.simple: The technology that guides US air traffic is decades old, and parts of it keep breaking. Each failure grounds thousands of flights and costs airlines and travelers. Fixing it will take a large federal spending package.
nyt.source: NYT via World in Summary / ABC7 Chicago

nyt.title: Lutnick pushed to weaken chip rules that overlap his family business
nyt.body: The Times reports Commerce Secretary Lutnick pushed to loosen chip rules touching his family's business interests. The timing is notable, since Commerce is expected to announce the AI 'national champions' list.
nyt.simple: Lutnick oversees export rules for advanced chips. A report that he pushed to relax rules affecting his family's interests raises conflict-of-interest questions. That could invite scrutiny of the coming AI export program and slow it down.

nyt.title: Iran strikes US base in Bahrain; mine claims near Hormuz
nyt.body: Iran hit a US helicopter base in Bahrain on Sunday, its first attack on a Gulf state in weeks, and state TV said five vessels struck mines. Brent stayed ≈$96 and briefly flipped from −0.9% to +0.46%.
nyt.simple: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway that carries a large share of the world's oil. Attacks near it usually lift oil prices, but traders saw this one as contained. If shipping is actually disrupted, gasoline and inflation would jump quickly.

talking_points.topic: Why Dec-27 SOFR moved more than Dec-26
talking_points.point: After CPI, the Dec-27 SOFR-implied rate rose ≈21.5bp versus ≈12bp for Dec-26. The market is pricing a longer hiking cycle, not just an earlier one. Ask a rates trader whether they would express a hawkish Warsh as a Dec26/Dec27 steepener in SOFR or as 2s10s, and how the 20Y auction tail risk changes that.

Gold is ≈$3,850, about 9% down YTD, with 10Y real yields near ≈2.9% and DXY at 103.5, the highest since Apr 2025. Even an Iranian strike on a US base couldn't lift it. A good question for a metals desk: when does central-bank buying become the marginal price-setter again, at what level of real yields?

BKX rose 0.6% on a day the Nasdaq fell 0.9%, because steeper curves help net interest margins. The risk sits on the other side of the balance sheet: AOCI (unrealized bond) losses and CRE refinancing, as with a Loop tower trading at a ≈75% discount. With Hancock Whitney–Trustmark at $3.2B, ask a commercial banker whether deal math still works when acquired securities books are marked down.

caveats: WSJ, NYT and Chicago Tribune were not directly accessible. Their stories come from press-digest and secondary coverage (MarketScreener, MLQ.ai, World in Summary), and the Tribune bucket uses Chicago Sun-Times, ABC7, Quartz and CME releases. Futures, gold, Brent, copper and silver are early-morning snapshots that differ across sources, so they are shown as ranges or ≈. The 2Y, 30Y and real-yield levels are Friday reads. SOFR-implied rates are post-CPI figures from Nov 10 and may have moved. Retail-sales consensus is carried over from prior calendars. Several data sites (Yahoo, Reuters mirrors) could not be fetched in this run.

updates.label: Close
updates.headline: The AI selloff spread into a broad close. The S&P 500 lost ≈1.8% to 7,427, the Nasdaq ≈2.5% and the Dow 659 points, while Treasuries only edged ≈3bp richer and gold slid to a 13-month low, so bonds still aren't hedging stocks going into retail sales and Nvidia.
points: Close: S&P 500 7,427.40 (−134.27, ≈−1.78%), Dow 51,688.96 (−659.41, ≈−1.26%), Nasdaq Comp ≈24,510 (≈−2.49%; sources range 24,510–24,614). That is the S&P's third straight loss, and all three indexes finished well below their noon levels. NVDA fell ≈4.2%. Late selling spread beyond AI names into financials, a point to watch for the KBW bank index. No Russell 2000 close found.

Rates: the 10Y finished ≈5.12% (≈−3bp; Fri high 5.174%), the 2Y ≈4.82–4.85% (≈−1 to −5bp) and the 30Y ≈5.47% (≈−1bp). The 2s10s spread is a touch steeper at ≈+27–30bp. A 1.8% equity drop bought only a few basis points of rally, which is the morning thesis confirmed: inflation and supply risk are capping duration's hedge value. Dec +25bp is still ≈88–94% with no new Fed signal.

Warsh: no coverage of the ≈2:15 PM CT fireside chat was available by publication time, so there's nothing to add to the midday read (scenarios, not forecasts; no December hint). The FT reported that Huang allies may lobby for his return while Nvidia's board reportedly isn't planning it, which raises headline risk into Tuesday's print.

Metals/FX: spot gold ≈$3,848 (−0.8%, Reuters via Polandinsight, 1:47 PM ET) after touching $3,830.74, its lowest in more than a year and ≈31% below January's record. DXY ≈103.5, still at a 19-month high. No reliable settles found for silver, copper or crude; the tiles keep midday reads (silver ≈$47, LME copper ≈$13,290/t, WTI ≈$88, Brent ≈$95–97).

Tomorrow (Tue, CT): 7:30 AM Oct retail sales (cons ≈+0.2% m/m, control ≈+0.4%; prior +0.8%), 8:15 AM industrial production, 9:00 AM NAHB (prior 29, moved from today). Nvidia FQ3 comes after the close with an implied move of ≈8–11%. The 13F deadline was tonight, and Berkshire's Q3 holdings land after hours.
updates.simple: Stocks had a rough day. Investors dumped computer-chip and AI companies, worried about Nvidia's leadership turmoil before its earnings report on Tuesday, and by the end of the day the selling had spread to banks too. Usually when stocks fall, people buy government bonds as a safe place, which pushes yields (the interest rate bonds pay) down a lot, but today yields barely fell. That's a sign investors are still worried about inflation and more Fed rate hikes. Gold kept falling because a strong dollar and high yields make a metal that pays no interest less attractive.

updates.label: Midday
updates.headline: Warsh gave no December signal and set out AI scenarios from a productivity boom to an equity bust, while the chip rout deepened. By noon ET the Nasdaq was ≈−1.7% and the S&P ≈−1.1%, and the 10Y held at ≈5.13–5.15%.
points: Warsh (11:00 AM CT, SF Fed): he described AI outcomes as 'illustrative scenarios, not forecasts.' The upside case is faster real growth with employment near full capacity. The downside case is that the boom disappoints, stocks bust, and the economy recovers 'without the productivity gains' (CNBC, Axios). He declined to comment on near-term policy or December, so the morning's 'productivity vs overheating' test came out a draw. Dec +25bp pricing is still ≈88–94% depending on the source.

Equities at 12:00 PM ET: S&P 500 −1.14% (≈7,476), Nasdaq Comp −1.72% (≈24,700), Dow −0.83% (≈51,900); levels are derived from Friday's closes. The Dow gave up the open's rotation cushion (−0.15%). A chip gauge was −4.5% and NVDA ≈−2.4% before Tuesday's print.

Rates: the 10Y is ≈5.13–5.15% (sources differ), essentially unchanged from the post-open level. The curve is approximately 2Y ≈4.86%, 5Y ≈4.97% and 30Y ≈5.46%, but those timestamps are unconfirmed. The equity selloff hasn't produced a flight-to-quality bid, so stocks and bonds are not hedging each other at these yields. Barr and Williams are also on today's Fedspeak list.

Cross-asset: gold ≈$3,865 (Fortune 9 AM ET read, inside a $3,832–3,902 range), silver ≈$47.1 (≈−3%), LME copper ≈$13,290/t, Brent ≈$95–97, WTI ≈$88, DXY ≈103.4–103.5. Moves since the open are small. Metals remain pinned by the dollar, the 5% 10Y and the China miss.

Correction to the morning calendar: the November NAHB index is listed for Tue Nov 17, 9:00 AM CT (Forex Factory, Investing.com), not today. The prior reading is 29, a 14-year low. No new bank or deal headlines since the UniCredit–Commerzbank clearance. Still ahead: Warsh's ≈2:15 PM CT fireside chat and the 13F deadline after the close.
updates.simple: The Fed chair spoke about artificial intelligence and laid out several possible futures: AI could make workers far more productive, or the hype could fade and stocks could crash. He refused to say what the Fed will do with interest rates in December, so bond markets barely moved. Stocks kept falling as investors sold chip companies before Nvidia's earnings on Tuesday, and gold and silver stayed low because a strong dollar and high interest rates make non-interest-paying metals less attractive.

updates.label: Post-open
updates.headline: Empire State collapsed to 7.8 from 25.5 (consensus ≈17–18) with prices paid down 14 points, nudging the 10Y about 2bp lower to ≈5.13%, but the open is all about AI: Nasdaq −1.1–1.5%, chips −4–6% before Nvidia.
points: Empire State (Nov): headline 7.8, versus 25.5 in October and ≈16.7–17.6 expected. New orders fell to 3.0 from 23.2. Prices paid dropped 14 points to 45.9 (from 59.5), and prices received eased to ≈27.2 (from 30.6). Employment rose to 18.1 (from 10.3), its best in about four years, and the six-month outlook improved 8 points to 28.9.

Rates: the 10Y is ≈5.131%, down ≈2bp, after Friday's 5.174% high (CNBC). This is the first cooler price signal since CPI/PPI, but one regional survey won't move the Fed. One FedWatch read puts Dec +25bp at ≈88.5%, below the morning's ≈93–94%, with the rest on 50bp. 2Y and 30Y readings for today weren't available (Fri: 4.86% and ≈5.47%).

updates.simple: The New York Fed asks local factories each month whether business is getting better or worse. November's answer was 'a lot less better than last month', and fewer factories said their costs are rising quickly. That's slightly good news on inflation, so bond yields (the interest rate the government pays to borrow) dipped a bit. But stocks fell anyway because investors are selling chip makers like Nvidia before its earnings on Tuesday.
